General.Description:
The Morland estate has been in decline for forty years. The house is maintained after a fashion; the grounds have largely returned to wilderness. The greenhouse — three hundred panes of Victorian glass enclosing a climate-controlled interior that maintains a constant tropical warmth regardless of the English weather outside — has never been neglected. Not once, in forty years. Not even in the winter that buried the rest of the estate under a metre of snow.

Eleanor Morland, returning to the family home for the first time in fifteen years to settle her father's estate, finds the greenhouse in perfect condition and her father's gardener — ancient, largely silent, comprehensively uncommunicative — still tending it with the devotion of a priesthood.

She also finds, in a locked room adjacent to the greenhouse, a collection of journals dating back eighty years. And a plant she cannot identify in any taxonomic reference she can access. And the growing sense that the history of the Morland family, as she has always understood it, is significantly incomplete.

The Glass Garden is a beautifully crafted gothic literary novel about the stories families keep hidden and the ones that eventually force themselves into the light. Isabelle Mortimer writes with the precision of a naturalist and the instincts of a storyteller who understands that the best secrets are the ones that have been hiding in plain sight.

Compelling, atmospheric, and deeply satisfying.
